utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, we noticed that the witness list has been changed again. It is a matter of concern because it's -- for all those concerned in the case, it means more and additional work. Could you please tell us what the effect of the changes are?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the document that notified the latest listing is dated the 22nd of August, but I gather that there was unfortunately some difficulty with getting the material to Your Honours. The plan, as I think I revealed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put that loudspeaker down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The plan, as I think I revealed a month ago, was that all remaining Albanian-speaking witnesses should be taken this week if at all possible, because after that we understand that the Albanian interpretation booth will no longer be manned. If you look at the witnesses that are numbered 1 to 16, they are the Albanian-speaking witnesses save one, number 4, who has to be called this week. Many of them are subject to 92 bis but not all. Indeed, two of the longer witnesses will be today, I think, numbers 2 and 3. But we recognise that it's a little optimistic to expect 16 witnesses to be done within the week, but we'll do our very best. And so there may be some Albanian-speaking witnesses at the beginning of next week. Starting at 17, there's a witness subject to, I think, of an application. There's then number 18 for whom there are particular problems, the subject of full applications made recently in relation to how his evidence will be available. Number 19 should not be a problem, I think. Twenty and 21 are obviously potentially substantial witnesses. Twenty-two is a witness who can be taken at any time, as it were, as a filler. And if I may, as it were, borrow Your Honours' experience, he's giving evidence as officer in the case tidying up various matters rather than giving evidence he was originally forecast to give. Number 23, I'm not sure of the prospects of that witness being available. I'll return to 24 in a minute. And the numbers 25 and 26 are witnesses whose evidence is necessary to call in light of the cross-examination of the earlier witness Karleusa. We are hopeful that they will be available. So those witnesses from 17 to 26 are bound, we would think, to take a week but we would hope not necessarily much more. And accordingly, by the time one reaches 26, allowing for the possibility that one or two of the witnesses may not be available, by the time one reaches 26, that's about two weeks or a little more of evidence gone subject to what I must say now about Witness 24. Witness 24, as the Court is aware, is the subject of a particular order. The Prosecution complied with that order as swiftly as it possibly could and has entered into constructive negotiations with one of the other parties involved in an application of which the Court is aware. That party has been not inconvenienced but facing the reality of vacation but has been complying and I think anxious to comply with the Court's orders and has been in negotiation with us. Those negotiations are not concluded, and I cannot be sure that they will be concluded in time for that witness to be called in this part of the trial. I'm doing my best, but there are not only negotiations, there are also orders of a government that have to be made before matters can be brought comprehensively to this court, and we'll do our very best and keep you informed. But without number 24 and noticing what there is to be said about numbers 27, 28, 29, and 30, my forecast is that we would take a little over two but by no means the full three weeks with a consequential advance in the start date of the other part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've now received a medical report on the health of the accused which we called for, a further report. That may have some impact on the speed of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is a document I don't think I've seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It has to be translated in any event. Well, let us begin the evidence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just make one other point for information? There is an outstanding issue about Rule 70. It arises, if we can look at our table, particularly in relation to Witness number 30. The Rule 70 issue is the subject of an application for reconsideration -- not reconsideration, for review, not just at the hand of the OTP but at the hand of the government. Rule 70 provision is on hold until that matter is determined substantially. No witnesses categorised by me as Rule 70, including number 30, will be available to me until after that issue is resolved. So number 30, although he relates strictly to Kosovo and only to Kosovo, is a witness who I won't be able to call in the Kosovo segment and will apply to call later if he becomes available. My forecast is that once this Rule 70 issue is determined, although things may look a little difficult at the moment, in fact issues will become clearer and the way ahead will become easier to map and probably easier to negotiate, but I'm afraid there is going to be a pause in Rule 70 matters until that issue is determined. I shall be here until Wednesday but probably not on Thursday and Friday, and the only witness who I can forecast might be moved from his present position, with leave of the Court, would be Mr. Merovci. He's here only to deal with the videotape of a television interview. So it's a very discrete matter. Once he and the tape are here, I might ask him to take earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how many potential Rule 70 witnesses do you have in the case as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: , I don't know the precise number in relation to the Croatia-Bosnia segment, but perhaps I can -- a large number, but they fall into different categories. There's the witness like witness number 30 who is, as it were, a straightforward and an ordinary witness. I don't mean that in any derogatory way, but who is at the -- in the view of the government concerned, surrounded with Rule 70 protection, and there are quite a large number of those witnesses and there has, therefore, to be resolution of how they are to be dealt with. There are then other witnesses of a much, again elevated is the wrong word, but of a much higher profile. There are several of those. In a way, they fall for different consideration and determination. They may have a very significant potential on the case. They are not immediately covered by the issues being covered by the issue for Rule 30, but judgement is that once the Rule -- once the witness 30 -- I beg your pardon, not the Rule, once the witness 30 is decided, it will be possible for us to look with a much clearer view as to how we're going to deal with all Rule 70 issues. So the long answer to Your Honour's question is: There are several witnesses, I'm not quite sure of the number of the witness 30 type, but then there's another Rule 70 category, really, which will fall possibly for separate and later consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course we use the term Rule 70 informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I'm not going to suggest that this amounts to any acknowledgement of the appropriateness of their being so described, but I take the point. Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld will be taking first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't translated, Mr. Milosevic. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to make a comment with regard to this list, and that is what you brought up, actually. It's not only the way you put it at the outset that we got a new list. Have you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the fault was mine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is not only that as you had observed at the outset, it is not only that we got a new list, I wish to underline that we got it on the last working day before this weekend. However, that is not the core of the matter that I wish to refer to. I have a few objections. Proposals are being made here for witnesses to hear people employed at the OTP as witnesses. That is to say that this is not really testimony in terms of presenting evidence. It can only constitute yet another element of carrying out the function of this false indictment. Namely, you have here witnesses such as Kevin Curtis and John Zdrilic who are employees of the OTP. That practically means that they are sitting on two different chairs at the same time. They are sitting at the Prosecution bench and they're also supposed to take the witness stand, and they are supposed to testify about their very own false indictment, and this is something that is quite unfamiliar to me in any kind of regular court proceedings or in any kind of regular type of court. So this is number 17 and number 22 respectively. Secondly, because I mean these are two elements. The indictment and the Prosecution are one thing, and here they appear in two different roles. It's as if Mr. Nice were to take the witness stand himself and if he were to testify just as his staff members are supposed to be doing. Secondly, in the statement of this purported witness, Kevin Curtis, we found out about some new facts which make it incumbent upon you gentlemen to look into the circumstances of the commission of crimes that were committed in order to have me brought here. He says in his statement that he allegedly arrested me, although I had already been arrested. So we cannot even talk about arrest; that the warden of the prison handed me over without any decision whatsoever; that he asked him for papers and that the other one respond that had he had no papers whatsoever. That is to say that in an illegal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. We will in due course consider the admissibility of this evidence. We're not going to decide it now. We have an application -- just a moment. We have an application in relation to Mr. Curtis's evidence which we've got to consider, and if we are going to allow that witness to give evidence, we will hear you first before we make any decision about that. Likewise, any objections to any of the other evidence we'll hear. But we're now going to hear the evidence which we've got here, the witnesses who are present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. May, since in the statement of that witness, irrespective of how you're going to rule, whether an employee of the OTP can be a witness as well or not, there are certain elements that make it incumbent upon you to do something because crimes were committed in terms of violating habeas corpus and other provisions of national law and international law. And you are duty-bound to take a stand with regard to this in keeping with international law, because in any normal court of law, if such crimes were committed, I would have to be released immediately. You can take any kind of stand you want, but you do have to take a stand, and you have to inform the public thereof and me as well, naturally. And the third objection I have is that I wish to say the following: I see that some new witnesses have been introduced now, Dragan Ilic, for example, Slobodan Borisavljevic, and we did not receive any statements that they had given. I don't know whether you have received any statements that they gave. There are no statements of theirs. Secondly, with regard to this third witness from the police, Bozidar Protic, there is also not a statement. There is only some kind of minutes of the working group of the Ministry of the Interior of this puppet government that is now in place in Belgrade. And for Caslav Golubovic we have a statement in English. He could not have possibly given it in English, only in Serbian, but we did not receive a statement in Serbian. Then also Zdrilic who is an employee of the OTP. So he cannot be a Prosecutor and a witness. He cannot write the indictment and then testify on behalf of that indictment. So we have here a list that was given in a totally unacceptable manner. So these are my objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will look into the question of statements. Any other questions we'll deal with when it's appropriate for the witnesses to give evidence. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's the Prosecution's intention to call Muharrem Dashi, and the proposal was that we deal with him by way of 92 bis with cross-examination. Your Honours, I am not aware whether the Court has in fact had an opportunity to provide us with a ruling on our application, and accordingly, I may ask you, before I call him, as to whether or not we may proceed in the way of 92 bis with this witness, he being with respect to Kacanik of which you've heard considerable other evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the application is for this witness, Mr. Dashi's evidence, to be given under Rule 92 bis. You will have the opportunity to cross-examine. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what my general position is with regard to these abbreviated witnesses who have been testifying according to this Rule of yours only in order to shorten the time I have for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit the statement. It is cumulative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would then ask that the usher bring in Muharrem Dashi. And while we're waiting for Mr. Dashi, Your Honours, this witness will be talking about events that occurred in the village of Stagovo in the municipality of Kacanik, and you may want to just have a look at the atlas, page 12, and I can perhaps show you where Stagovo is. At the intersection of line 20 near the top, if we go along the top, and line 80 down the side, you will see right at the intersection of those two lines where there is a railway line you get Stagovo

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just north of Kacanik city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, can you tell the Court how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I am 43 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, sir, is it true that you are a Kosovo Albanian Muslim from the village of Stagovo in the municipality of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And prior to the conflict in 1999, can you tell us about how many people inhabited Stagovo and what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: There were 1.620 people in Stagova, all Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I understand, sir, that you are married?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married, and I have four children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you are a professional engineer, but you have actually been employed as a teacher in the village of Stagovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, at some time on the 6th of June, 1999, did you provide a statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently, sir, on the 10th of March of this year, 2002, did you have an opportunity to have that statement read back to you and then appear before an officer of the Tribunal, a presiding officer, and confirm that the contents of that statement were true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that statement be marked as an exhibit in these proceedings, Your Honour, the bising package, so to speak. While that's being distributed, Your Honours, I propose to give a very brief summary of some of the highlights of what might be contained in that statement. Your Honours, the statement discloses that in the last two months of the conflict, Mr. Dashi served as a civilian member of a local KLA unit in the village Stagovo, in the municipality of Kacanik. As a civilian member, did he not bear arms but his duties included providing food and shelter for refugees that gathered in Stagovo. There were 15 members in the unit, and in early May 1999, they started a 24-hour watch for Serbian troops. The statement describes the actions of the Serb forces in the village of Stagovo, municipality of Kacanik, on the 21st of May, 1999, and following days. Now, on the morning of the attack, the 21st of May, the witness apparently was given a rifle and was assigned to an observation post. He was at that observation post on the morning of the 21st of May, together with two other members of the unit. At about 4.15 a.m., he observed soldiers advancing toward the village. The soldiers were wearing green camouflage VJ uniforms. They were all on foot and came from the direction of Kacanik i Vjeter, Stari Kacanik. The witness warned the other members of the KLA unit and they all went to a new observation point. He decided not to fight back for fear of putting civilians at further risk. They stayed in their position the whole day because the village was surrounded. The witness could hear mortars, automatic weapons, and other weapons being fired. The KLA did not return fire. He could also see a lot of smoke coming from the village. He observed different kinds of uniforms used by the forces and describes them in his statement, including VJ, police, and what he describes as paramilitaries. After the Serb forces withdrew, the witness entered the village with his unit and in an area called Kumulishta, he saw five bodies consisting of two grown men and three elderly women whom he names in his statement. He then went by a stream where he saw three more bodies and a short distance away he saw a further two bodies. In addition to seeing those particular 10 bodies, he heard that the bodies of two elderly men were found about 200 metres from the stream. In his statement he briefly describes some of the injuries he saw on the victims and then tells you that he went through the village and estimates that 60 per cent of the houses had been burned. He also saw that houses had been looted, windows in the school and the mosque had been broken, and livestock had been killed. The following day, that's the 22nd of May, the witness was together with his nephew, a Mr. Dullovi Naser when he made a video recording of the bodies. The bodies from filmed in the positions that they were found and later in the day, he participated in the burial of those bodies. Apparently the Serbs had mined the cemetery and exploding mines injured three people. On the 27th of May, the witness's nephew left Kosovo for Macedonia to join other members of his family who had fled before the Serb attack. That is the brief summary of that statement. Needless to say there are further details contained in it. I started reading before we actually had a number assigned to the statement. Might we have that now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's number 285.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless Your Honours have any questions, those would be my questions of Mr. Dashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when you were in secondary school, were there any problems in Kacanik regarding attendance in school?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I worked in Stagova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we saw on the map, this is practically at the very edge of Kacanik, and the teachers that you probably know, and you would also know what the situation was in your municipality, or perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't -- in your school, Mr. Dashi, can you help us with this: Were there any problems regarding attendance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no problems at all. The police came quite often, but we didn't have any great problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, during your schooling in Kacanik, did you have contacts with your peers from other schools?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't have any contacts either with Serbs or any other non-Albanian pupils from your school or other schools?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: There weren't any Serb pupils in Kacanik, whereas in Stagova there were Serb teachers who, to my great wonder, continued working there. They had been there earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which language did you teach in your school?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you know that since -- that out of 85 employees there were 62 Albanians in the municipality of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you taught in Albanian without any problems. So I'm asking you also if you know that in the Municipal Assembly, in the organs of local municipal power, the vast majority of employees in Kacanik were Albanians. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: That's true. This was earlier. The government in Kacanik went over to the Serbs, whereas the schools became private more or less, but I won't go on about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could the Serbs have taken over until the bombing, the 24th of March, when out of the total of 85 employees in the municipality, in the Municipal Assembly, 62 of them were Albanians? How could that have happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: The communal authorities, the municipal authorities, were completely Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So does that mean that what I am stating is not true? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: It's not true because in Kacanik the municipal authorities were run by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. But the important thing is that you claim that this is not true. But there are written records of this, so this is not in dispute. But please, can you tell me if you know whether in 1995, at the proposal of local authorities, a local police was formed exclusively from members of the Albanian and Romany ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "In 1998."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998? I don't know anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that 12 members of the local police were killed or kidnapped by the KLA, and they were all Albanians? And I think a couple of them were Romanies. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would it assist you if I were to read you the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: You can read them if you want, but I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even though I haven't even read them, you don't know them. So this is no need for me to read them then. Do you know that in the nearby villages, for example Kotlina and Ivaja, the KLA formed camps for members of the local police and for Albanians, citizens loyal to the state, loyal to the Republic of Serbia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far are Kotlina and Ivaja from your village? You're a teacher and you're interested in social events, things that are going on.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: That's true, but I don't know anything about that because I didn't have any specific competence in such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked how far away those villages are. Can you help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stagova to Kacanik is 6 kilometres, and it's about 8 from Ivaja to Kacanik, and 15 or 16 from Kotlina. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell me if you know that in this village of Ivaja, which is 8 kilometres away from Kacanik, that in a camp like that, a group of 15 Albanians was found and released, people who were kept there by the KLA? And they were released by the local police. Did you hear about this event?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You provided your statement on the 6th of June, 1999, the one that we're discussing now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in the camp. That's where I gave the declaration, the statement. The 26th was when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the KLA in the month of April 1999 or before that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: In April I wasn't a soldier. I wasn't a fighter because I didn't have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were a member of the KLA without a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was your function in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I was there to help the civilian population in the village, displaced persons who had arrived, to help them find shelter and to help them find food. That was what I was there to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this related only to accommodation and food in your village or did you go around neighbouring villages and perform those duties over a wider area?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Only in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as a member of the KLA, I assume that you know that on the 8th of April, 1999, at 1740 hours to be precise, a terrorist attack was carried out by 20 armed terrorists of the KLA against the police in the street of Bora Vukmirovic in Kacanik. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, Serb forces entered Stagova, and on that day a house was burned, the one of Rufik Krraba and the population fled to the hills. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the attack of this terrorist group numbering 20 terrorists against the police station in Kacanik on that date, but you do know that they came to Stagovo; is that right? You don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Serb forces -- Serb forces entered Stagova in the morning. They fired three grenades in the evening into my neighbourhood where I lived. And there was only one house burnt on the 8th of April. There were no other major crimes committed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that date, on the 8th of April, nine police officers were wounded there? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: There weren't any injured in Stagova. I don't know exactly, and that's why I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far did you say that Stagovo is far from Kacanik, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Six kilometres. So you don't know anything about this, and you don't know that nine police officers were wounded, and you don't know who fired at those police officers. So I assume I don't even need to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. This is nothing new. And do you know that in the village of Doganovic five children were killed by a cluster bomb, a NATO cluster bomb? They were all from the Koqa family. An Albanian man, Sekbija Koqa [phoen], a statement explained that the children had found a cluster bomb, tried to open it, and were killed. The names were Fisnik Koqa, Valdet Koqa, Burim Koqa, Edem Koqa and Osman Koqa, and the following persons were wounded: Besnik and Avdija. They were all from the village of Doganovic. The children were born in 1990, 1984, 1985.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch the rest of the birth years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about that event? You're a teacher. This is something involving children. Do you know about this event?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But how they were killed, we know it was a bomb, but whether it was a NATO bomb or some other bomb, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was the name of the commander of the KLA unit that you belonged to? Do you know that at least?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: It was a very small organisation. To tell you the truth, in Stagova it was the people who organised the unit themselves as part of the army. It was all the people, the citizens. Whether people were civilians or fighters, they would suffer the same fate from Serb forces. And that's why some people were able to find arms. The only reason was not only to fight, to fight the police or the army, but at least to survive a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't respond to my question, what was the name of the commander of the unit that you belonged to. I see that you have a different story. So I'm just asking you about this specific fact.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Remzi Krraba was the name, who was responsible for that unit. Krraba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Krraba. And was this unit of yours part of a larger unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't really have any information, any detailed information, on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You became an observer, as far as I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I was a civilian observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean a civilian, when you yourself said that you had a rifle when you were at the observation post. Is a civilian with a rifle still a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We -- there were four of us, and we shared a rifle. It was a very old rifle. Not very good, but we used it in four different shifts. So it wasn't really my rifle or didn't belong to anyone specifically. But we -- we kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I am familiar that rifle, because I used it when I was serving in the army. It can kill at 1.800 metres. It's a 7.9 millimetre calibre rifle. And on page 3 of your statement, you say that you were armed with a machine-gun, a Kalashnikov, and mortars. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes. There was a mortar and Kalashnikov, and there was a machine-gun. There were machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said a couple of semi-automatics. Can one be a couple of semi-automatics?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: There was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's say Kalashnikovs, mortars, and semi-automatic weapons. Where did you obtain them?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Because I couldn't find proper weapons, I wasn't able to. Where the others got their weapons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How many people did you kill with the weapons that you have just listed? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can say very honestly that no bullet ever killed anyone and was ever fired by me from this -- from these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's say that it's true that you didn't kill anybody, that you fired into the air. Do you have any idea how many people were killed from those weapons by the other members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? Or sorry, I will repeat. I did not fire my weapons that -- my weapon that day, and no one was killed. No one fired weapons. Not only I did not fire, but no other fighter fired a weapon that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether you have any information about what it was that resulted in the death of those nine police officers on that day? Was it perhaps some other KLA group that fired them and not yours? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that at 4.00 a.m. you were at the observation post. Was it dark?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: It was dark, yes. And then after 4.00, we could sort of see things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, you saw people who were walking towards Stagovo. From what distance did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: From the main road where the Serb forces entered near the cemetery near old Kacanik. It was difficult to see down there, whereas we could see the other forces coming on the road from Kacanik. It was about 400 metres away, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw that these soldiers were firing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: At the beginning, they weren't firing. They merely took up their positions after the Gudaq neighbourhood and that was all, and we would observe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, were they -- did members of the KLA fire at them?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did anybody shoot from the position of those 15 men that you joined if you did not open fire at them then?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's try to understand this. In your village, your group of the KLA, that is one element, mortar, machine-gun, Kalashnikov, et cetera. You took up positions. Soldiers were shooting, and you did not respond. Who were the soldiers shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslav soldiers. Who were they shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat: The Serbian forces didn't fire until about six hours after they took up their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When they took up positions -- I mean, what does that mean, "After six hours"? Were they at positions for six hours or was all of this taking place at 6.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: After 6.00 in the morning, there was a lot of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that you think that the Serbs were shooting in order to keep people in the village and to prevent aid from reaching the villagers. That's what your statement says, and that is your claim. That is what you claim the reason was for their shooting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: On that day -- this sentence may not be accurate, because what happened was the soldiers kept the village surrounded, and the remainder of the police, of whom we were not aware, came -- came from the area of Vitia, and they captured the citizens and murdered them and executed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that you remained at these positions and that you could not move at all so that the soldiers could not see you, and that from your positions you could not see any other members of the security forces. Is that what you stated or not? Is that the way it was or is that not the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Of course the positions where we were, we couldn't see the forces which we suppose came from Vitia. We suppose that's where they came from. They were stationed in the hills up there. And we didn't know what was happening in Kumulishta or at the stream where the civilians were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, how can you know what was going on and who was shooting at whom when you were hidden all the time and when you yourself have been saying now that you didn't see a thing?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I didn't intend to enter into details here. The important thing is this population was massacred. However, from the position where I was, you could see clearly the terrain at that side of Stagova where the school, the mosque, and the library and other things are. I didn't emphasise it in my declaration, but I can tell you now. There was a car. I don't know what kind of registration, but it was a light colour, and it was seen from the position where I was, and it went from the train station to the school. There were weapons, no doubt a Gulinov. They were positioned in it. And throughout this time, it moved from the station to the school and it was firing all the time. I didn't see the massacre actually happening, but it states in my statement that the place was so hidden. But the truth was that Serbian forces massacred members of the population. And I say this because in that part, in that area, there were no forces of ours at all, and there was no provocation of the Serbian army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You keep using this word "massacre," that Walker brought into fashion. That is to say when there is a conflict between the KLA and the army and police, if the police kills a member of the KLA, then that's a massacre. And what do you call it -- what do you qualify as the following: When the KLA kills a policeman. Is that also a massacre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for your statement, I'm going to quote it to you. I'm going to quote only a few pearls from your statement. This is how a sentence of yours reads: "I think that Ibrahim's wife saw how all three of them were killed." You think that Ibrahim's wife saw this. And then towards the end of paragraph, and all this is on page 4, you say "200 the metres away, that the bodies of two elderly men were found. I was told the next day, but I never saw the bodies myself." What are you testifying about? Please. You were at an observation point, and you didn't see a thing. On the other hand, you say that you think that Ibrahim's wife saw some kind of execution, and then you say what you heard the following day. What are you testifying about, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I'm testifying to the massacre that took place in Stagova on the 21st. I saw the bodies. They were very close to one another. So the furthest away was 10 or 15 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you say all of that, do you know that precisely in Stagovo, because you say you're not familiar with anything else except for Stagovo, well, this was precisely in Stagovo, your village, on the 22nd, that is to say the following day, a soldier by the name of Goran Stankovic was killed. You've got to know that because you say you stayed there until the 27th. On the 22nd in Stagovo a soldier was killed. So does that show that there was fighting or that there was no fighting? And did the Serb soldiers perhaps kill that soldier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question. Do you know that a soldier was killed the next day, the 22nd? Mr. Dashi, would you deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 22nd, we filmed the bodies, and we have the recording. And as for this soldier or policeman who is said to have been killed, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about it, do you? You don't know who killed this soldier. You don't know that he was killed at all; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: If I knew, I would testify to it, but I don't know about it. On the 22nd, the bodies were buried and the film was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is this recording of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I have it with me. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is there on this film? I did not receive this. Please, what is there on this film?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: It shows all the bodies that were found there, and they were filmed when they were buried. Then there is a film of burnt houses and livestock that were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many burnt houses can be seen? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: The statistics are over 60 per cent, but I don't know how many the film shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't you take pictures of these houses that were burned? You didn't miss taking pictures of these houses if 60 per cent were burned.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: That's true, because we filmed the bodies from the -- and then merely filmed the area round the cemetery to show the situation that we were in and to show the type of thing that was done. We weren't making this film for the Tribunal, because we were in a very difficult position and didn't know really what we were doing. It was something happened -- that happened spontaneously, without any organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing to be organised. Over the past ten or 15 years, usually funerals are recorded either by camera or by video recorder. So you actually filmed the funeral. That is what you're referring to, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: That's quite true, because Stagova is a very scattered village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes -- wait a moment. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just thought I'd indicate that the Prosecution is aware that this -- the witness brought this video with him. It is available. We didn't introduce it into evidence because we have the narrative in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But if there is a question about it, it is available and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ryneveld, let us not waste more time. Let us move on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. The witness has given his evidence about the events and it's that that we'll rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, you say in your statement that you saw one house in flames. That is what your statement says on page 3. How did you come up with this figure of 60 per cent of all houses being burned now?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No doubt the statement refers to the time, 9.00, when we saw the first house being burned, and that is the first house being burnt at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you were being asked was: How did you come to the conclusion that 60 per cent of the houses were burnt? You may be able to answer that very simply, but would you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying 60 per cent but over 60 per cent if you analyse it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you count them? I mean, how did you come to that figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are 182 houses in Stagova. Ninety-six were burnt entirely, and 30 were partly burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, when were these houses burned?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: They were burned on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All 96 houses that you claim were burned were burned on the 21st, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they torched? Did somebody set fire to these houses or did they catch fire during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: There was no fighting. Let me tell you again. The houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain -- how do you explain, Mr. Dashi, the fact that, for example, throughout the war nobody moved out of Stari Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't understand. Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up with this witness. Can you -- You were asked about Stari Kacanik. Can you help about that? It's suggested that nobody moved out of there during the war. Can you help us about Stari Kacanik or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was the police station in Kacanik i Vjeter. I mean that it had been there a long time. And the only way out, the only route for evacuation, was through Kumulishta. And there the citizenry met their fate and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask another question if you want to clarify that, Mr. Milosevic, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you going to say that people were killed there as well in Kacanik? Do you know that in Kacanik, as a matter of fact, an Albanian party was formed, the Albanian Democratic Initiative? Do you know the name of Faik Jashari who was a member of the delegation in Rambouillet? He was from Kacanik, head of this party. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, your time is up now. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, I would kindly ask you for a few clarifications only related to your statement, the one that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal. In your statement, you said that you were mobilised. Does that mean that against your own will you became a member of the KLA or did you voluntarily join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I wasn't a volunteer for the KLA, but that was only because there were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further on you said in your statement that in your village that unit had 15 men altogether. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that or thereabouts. On the 21st I was with them, but I didn't actually count how many were there. We didn't have time to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did any one of you from that unit have a uniform, a KLA uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I didn't have one, and the great majority didn't have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is the other thing you said correct too, that this unit of yours was known as the 162nd Unit? Does that mean that there were 161 units before you that comprised what the KLA was? Was your unit the 162nd in line? Is that what this means?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: No doubt this might be an interpretation mistake, because the -- the 162nd Brigade was the brigade of the entire municipality of Kacanik. It was a unit in Stagova with the numbers that I've been talking about, which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you not know, then, this 162nd Brigade, how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the name of this brigade was Agim Bajrami, that it bore his name, and that he was killed in the fighting with Serb forces a year beforehand. So can you tell me, in 1998, how much fighting was there between the KLA and the Serb forces, as you had put it here? Was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: When Agim Bajrami was killed, there was no fighting as far as I know. Agim Bajrami was killed in the village of Gabrice. That's all I know. Killed by Serbian forces, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we clarify something that remained unclear a few minutes ago. You said that you carried a M-48 rifle on the 21st of May, 1999, at that observation post. You said in your first statement that on that day you were armed with machine-guns, Kalashnikovs, and a single mortar. And then on the 10th of March this year, you stated to the investigators here that you have to correct your statement, and you said the following, and I quote: "We were armed with one machine-gun, Kalashnikovs, and one mortar." Does that mean that each and every one of you on that day had a Kalashnikov? Because you were quite unequivocal that there was one machine-gun, one mortar, and Kalashnikovs. That's what you said on the 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: The truth is there was one mortar, one semi-automatic, and the remaining weapons were Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all of you have Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: Yes. There was one semi-automatic, one with a projectile, and the others were Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And if you could explain just one more thing to me. You were observing from that post of yours and you saw that the Serb forces were coming nearer. When you noticed this, you informed Muhamet and Shabedin Dashi and you sent them to the village to warn the rest of your unit about that; is that correct? Do you know whether they all withdrew from the village or did somebody remain in the village unarmed?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I reported this because there were a lot of civilians in Stagova. In my own neighbourhood, the houses were full of people and cousins and nephews and nieces from a neighbouring village called Biqek. My own neighbourhood was crammed with civilians. This was why Shabedin went and woke him up, because it was very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. In your particulars when you were questioned, you said that you were a refugee and that your present occupation is refugee and your previous occupation is engineer. Could you please explain to me why you left Kosovo on the 27th of May. Did somebody demand or request that you leave Kosovo on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI
utterances.text: I was not forced by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing re-arising. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. The Court will now adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sadik Xhemajli is the next witness. The Court has already had access to his statements because he was the subject of an application for 92 bis, but the Court decided that he should give evidence in full by its order, I think on the 2nd of August. There is a summary provided. There's a little additional evidence that I'm going to ask him to deal with via a video that's being prepared at the moment, and I'll explain that when we reach it. This witness's evidence will fit together with other evidence, in particular Dr. Loshi, who is coming later in the week and who, although he's a 92 bis witness or probably is a 92 bis witness himself, will produce a video showing the bodies involved in this particular killing and therefore, I shan't need to deal with this witness with a video that covers that topic. I should say that the witness wears darkened spectacles. He wears them at all times on medical advice. I have asked him if he can dispense with them for the purpose of giving evidence, but apparently not. And indeed I've seen a large number of photographs of him which I needn't produce to you but photographs of him in the performance of his duties, and he is at all times wearing the same spectacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that the piece of paper with the witness's name be placed on the overhead projector over the map just so that the members of the press can spell the name correctly if they wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your name Sadik Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Born in Izbica in the municipality of Skenderaj?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Living in Runik.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now having, I hope, given the press enough time to look at the spelling of the name, can we take that piece of paper off the overhead projector? And if we look at the map which is before us, we can see Skenderaj to the left, pretty well dead centre, I suppose, of the screen is Izbica, and the village where you lived a lot of your time is further to the north.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you are a married man with children?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the war how many houses were there in Izbica? What was the approximate population?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were 68 houses before the war, inhabited. Eight hundred and sixty people approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ethnic composition, please?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You in your statement deal with changes in the lives of Albanians following the removal of Kosovo autonomy. The learned Judges have heard a great deal about that, and I'm only going to ask you to deal with two short matters. First, following the change in autonomous status, what was the practical positions so far as carrying identification documents was concerned?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: True autonomy was taken away in 1989. Serbian regime had every document in Serbian and everything was written in Cyrillic with additions to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Who had to carry identification documents, everybody of all ethnicities or just some?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: This was valid for everybody, but in fact Serbs were never mistreated. But Albanians were forced to carry Serbian documents because they would get mistreated on the streets, in traffic, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second short point: In that same period of time when Albanian babies were born and named, was there something about the names they were given that reflected the change in status of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard from people that names such as Shqiponja, Flamur and Elbasan were not accepted by the Registrars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what sort of names were accepted?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Sadik, but they didn't allow names after national symbols, cities, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the names that they were to use instead, were they Serbian names or names that were more like Serbian or were they Albanian names?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were Albanian names but not involving national symbols or any special meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want now to turn to the KLA. On the 28th of November of 1997 - this is in the statement but not in the summary - was there the funeral of an Albanian teacher in the village called Llausha?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the teacher Halit Geci was killed by Serbian forces in the schoolyard. And more than 100.000, 200.000 people took part in the funeral and that was where the KLA appeared in public for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many members of the KLA appeared on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Some spoke, and how many others there were, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Llausha can be found if we withdraw the camera a little or -- on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's there near Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just -- thank you very much. You have to look on the right-hand page. It's difficult to see. It's there. It's immediately under the right-hand page where Skenderaj is shown.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There it is, just near Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Putting things in a chronological order, was there on the 28th of February of 1998 at Likoshane and Cirez a killing of villagers followed by a funeral with a large attendance of mourners?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. In Likoshan and Cirez there were 24 people in all killed, and great -- I took part in the funeral. Not as a soldier but as a citizen. There were more than half a million people present at those funerals, about 600.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was it following that second funeral on a date in March 1998 that you became a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No. After the murder of the legendary Commander Adem Jashari, I joined the KLA on the 13th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will deal with your involvement in the KLA briefly. The accused, if relevant, may have further questions. But did you have no previous military experience?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the unit that you were initially attached to a small one?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It was a very small unit, and there were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, there was no -- there was no conscription.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you initially armed or without arms?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: At the beginning, we didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the beginning did you have uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you in due course rise to the position of commander of your small unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I was a private to begin, and then a lieutenant, and at the end of the war I was an officer in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your unit was or became part of the 112th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to deal with the Padaliste and Qitak incident in May of 1998 but just in a couple of sentences, please. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1998, Serb police from the area of Istog attacked Padalishte with several tanks and burned several houses in Qitak, and the population were obliged to flee the village and head for the surrounding hills. And on the same day, there were two killed. That's Muhamet Shaban Citaku and Rifat Citaku, who was at 28 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see Padaliste on the map. It's a little out the focus. It's to the west and just slightly north of Skenderaj. But if we go further north on the map we come to a town or village Suhogerlle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Suhogerlle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And further to the north?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Padaliste is just where your finger is now. No, it's not. It's to the right. And the other town, if we can look further to the north -- there's Padaliste. Thank you very much. Now can we go north up that road, please, if the booth would you so good. Thank you very much. And the town now at the top of the screen, can you just -- that's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's a village. It's called Suhogerlle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you omitted from your statement and realised you omitted from it something about this village. In a sentence, what was it that you were aware of happening there?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: In this village, on the 5th, the 6th, and the 7th, the Serbs shelled incessantly to force the inhabitants of Suhogerlle to flee because this village is next to Banja, which is a Serbian village, whereas in Suhogerlle there is only one neighbourhood that is Serbian. And on -- there were six people, six civilians, not one of them in uniform, were killed in Suhogerlle. And three of them are still missing. They are Osman Osmani and Rexhep Zogaj and one other who are still counted missing and have never been found. On that occasion they kidnapped more than 40 people and it was led by Martic and together with local Serbs, and they took them to another Serbian village Cerkolez where they mistreated them and beat them, and then some of them they were then released. And then until the entry of NATO, not a single Albanian was allowed into that village. And they burned all the Albanian houses in the village of Suhogerlle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to the time when OSCE arrived, did you witness something of an attack on your own village of Runik involving airborne troops or use of airborne weaponry?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There was nothing like that after the OSCE came. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There was an air attack on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what sort of air -- airborne attack was it? What weapons were used?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1998, I -- as I explained, the first attack was on Padalishte, and we buried those two people who were killed, and they were buried next to the paved road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: And on the 18th of May, other forces came and used helicopters. And they were above Dubrava near Istog, and they would come above a house and fire with semi-automatic rifles. Two people were killed, Ramadan Loshi, 62, and Ramadan Citaku, 69. And Husein Citaku was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted you to help us on that. The OSCE arrived in October 1998 and withdrew on the 17th of March, 1999. While they were present, did the KLA cooperate with them or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: We had good relations with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did attacks by Serbs continue during the time of the OSCE presence? Did they increase? Did they decline in numbers?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It was relatively calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Following the departure of the OSCE, the NATO bombing began. In general, was it welcomed by the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The NATO bombing was supported by the Albanians because they were in danger. The entire population was in danger. The NATO bombing began on 24th of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: -- 1999, and on the 25th, Serbian forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, I know there is much you want to tell us, but as you realise, time is limited, and that involves every witness, I'm afraid. So could you concentrate both in this examination and in the cross-examination on the questions that you're asked and just answer them. If you need to make further explanation, no doubt you can in due course, but we do need to get through this evidence as expeditiously as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to hear, Mr. Xhemajli, this week from a witness who deals with killings that occurred at or near Padaliste of a family by the name of Imeraj. You've shown on the map the places where you were based, the places where you were born and the places where you were operating in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just help us with this single question? Were there any members of the Imeraj families involved with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And had there been, would you have known about it given the scale of the geography and your involvement?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, because they are also in-laws of mine. My -- my nephew was -- my niece was killed, my in-laws -- many of my in-laws were killed and 11 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We turn now to the central part of your evidence which is the incident at Izbica itself. It may be that it will be easier for you if Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8852 to 8860. you can do it slowly and with a pointer that the usher will give you to give a description of what happened by reference to the map. You can also do it verbally if you find that easier. The pointer is coming your way but -- use a pencil. The proper pointer seems to have vanished in the course of the summer. The incident at Izbica started on what date?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The events at Izbica started at 4.00 in the afternoon on 27th of March and went on until the 30th, until 9.45 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we look at what happened, where were you? What view did you have of events, please?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I was in the southern part, in the south-western part. I was on a hill in a wood, and from this point I saw various things that the Serbs did, how they entered, how they came to the meadow, and how they started shelling from all sides so that the people were forced to go out onto the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a second. At what distance were you viewing events and were you viewing them with an unaided eye or with the advantage of binoculars?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The -- the case happening to the south I saw with binoculars and towards to the west, but what was happening in the east I didn't see very well, but what happened in the east was further away from me, more than a thousand metres away and I couldn't see so clearly. Whereas the events that happened to the south were only 500 or 600 metres away. South-west I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Take your time, look at the map, and indicate with the pen, if you can, where you were positioned approximately, and then I'll ask the booth to focus in on that area of the map.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Here's Izbica. I was in this part down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we know from your statement that you're going to give an account of people gathering or being compelled to gather in Izbica itself. What led up to that gathering of people in Izbica? And use the map as you find convenient, but do it very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The people started gathering at Izbica as people left Padalishte, Leqina, Kastriot, and Citak and other places when they started leaving their villages, and they gathered to the south of Izbica and Serbian forces came at 4.00 in the afternoon on the 27th. And on the 28th --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. What caused these people to leave their various villages? As far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Because of the killings, the bombings, the shelling the inhabitants had to leave their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were the forces positioned that were shelling these surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Arriving from the west and east, and some came from the north and came down the asphalted road from Mitrovica. That's how most of them came. And all those villages that had been caught beforehand, all the population came towards Izbica thinking they would find safety there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. I didn't ask the question clearly enough. The forces that were shelling these various villages, where were those forces themselves positioned? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were on the hill of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you point that out to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Above the Meraj neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point that out, please?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Leqina, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To the south and west of the area shells were coming at different villages and the various villagers were gathering in a field to the south of Izbica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, because of the shelling. They gathered in a meadow because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They gathered in the meadow. Was this choice of the meadow and -- a natural act of the individuals or was there any question of them being led or herded by soldiers or other forces into that particular meadow?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Merely because it was a big field, and the people found it themselves. Nobody ordered them to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And had Izbica itself been being shelled or did it appear to be free from shelling?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, Izbica came under shell-fire from all sides too, and the people had to gather in that meadow. These were elderly people, women, children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again. Before the 28th of March and while people were gathering in the meadow at Izbica, was Izbica free of shelling?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It -- originally it was, but it was only on the 27th, starting at 4.00 that the encirclement surrounded coming from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on then. The people are now in the meadow at Izbica. Are you able to give an estimate of the number of people who were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Four thousand five hundred to 5.000. That's the general number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At about noon on the 28th what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Serbian forces came in uniforms and entered with tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us with the types of uniforms and what they signified as to the units involved?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were blue, camouflaged, and they went to the population and they divide -- they separated all the men one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing at a time, Mr. Xhemajli. To you, what units were signified by the uniforms worn by the forces you saw? Were they soldiers, police, or something else? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were soldiers and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other groupings?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Excuse me? Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other groups apart from regular --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. There were other kinds of uniforms but fewer of them. There were some paramilitaries, but mainly it was the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You should have observed that the 28th of March was a particular day in the Muslim calendar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. That day it was the day of the Bajram festival, and it was exactly on the day of Bajram that the Serbian forces carried out this massacre. They separated the men from the women, one by one, and lined them up towards the west. And after lining them up, all the men, a Serbian leader in uniform had -- separated out the younger children, age 12 to 14, and lined them up too. This is according to what the children say. And when another police commander came, he released the children, but they sent the men off in two directions; one towards the east and another group to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to pause there for a second. What you're telling us at this stage, is this something you saw yourself from a distance or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I saw the men being separated by the Serbian forces, but I didn't know about the children. I didn't see them. But I heard that they were separated too but were released by a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were told of that later by someone else?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. About the children, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
