utterances.text: Again, before we move on but to try to keep things in a chronological order so far as we can, just yes or no to this question: Have you been told by people who survived, or who were down in the field, of things that were being said by police and soldiers when they came to the field and surrounded them? Just yes or no, have you been told those things?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you been told, similarly, of what was being done by the soldiers to the people generally before the men were separated out and before the killings that you'll tell us in due course occurred? Have you been told what the police and soldiers did to the people?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: When they divided the men, they -- they insulted them, and they insulted NATO and Clinton and Rugova and Thaci, and they were also robbed. Both the men and the women were robbed. And it's said, according to accounts, that they took away over 500.000 marks that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on now to what happened to the men who had been separated, but before we take from you the detail, did you see any of this yourself directly or not? What actually happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the western side, these incidents I saw for myself. I saw 39 people being executed, with my own eyes. But the -- there were two other groups of ten and 15, and they were a little further, and they were all executed but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: And also, I was about 500 to 600 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then so far as the group you did see being executed is concerned, very briefly, what was it that you saw happen, please?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the western side, when they brought this group of men, a section of them arrived at a -- at a meadow, and they were executed by semi-automatic rifles at a distance of about five or six metres. They were all executed. There were -- in that group of people, there were elderly people, handicapped people with walking sticks, and there was elderly man who had two walking sticks, and he was executed. And there were mentally ill people who were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to -- thank you. I'll get you to give a little more detail about the composition of the group of people who were killed later. Did you receive -- just yes or no, please, to this question: Did you receive accounts from others of how the other two groups of men, whom you did not see, were executed? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No. I only heard -- I only heard the weapons. But later on, we found them killed. And they showed me -- and the survivor witnesses showed me their bodies in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While those executions were taking place, what were the remaining soldiers and policemen doing in the field, in particular in relation to cars and tractors?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They separated the men and sent them east and west, and then they -- they sent the women off in a convoy southward towards Albania, but they didn't allow them even to take bread with them. And they couldn't take anything with them, not even children's blankets. And then they piled them all up and burnt them on tractors and trailers and cars. And one trailer was left on the meadow, and Zoje Osmani, an elderly woman, was left on this trailer. She was unable to move, and she was burned alive. And Qerime Hajra from Izbica, who was in a wheelchair, was burned in the lower part of her body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've -- pause there. I want to deal with things in an orderly way and you're being very helpful, but let's just move on a little. In due course, you identified - indeed, I think probably spoke to - a number of survivors of this massacre or these massacres who were able to give or would be able to give eyewitness testimony.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, I've talked to them, the survivor witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've listed them in the statement you've made to the OTP. It's at page 6. And in addition to the names that you have listed there, another man Feka Fekaj, I think, you discovered had survived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Could you repeat that again, please? Could you repeat that name again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Feka Fekaj.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Ah, Feka Fekaj from Klina. He said two weeks ago that he was present at the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't propose to list the survivors. They are available to the accused and the amici if they need to contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the survivors spoke to you of one of the policemen who declined to carry out the executions and was replaced by somebody else who was willing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. It's said by Nasim Mulej from Jashanica, who had spoken to Jetish Qallapeku, and it was him who talked about this event. This policeman --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need from you on that, thank you very much. How long did the police and military forces stay in Izbica until withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Excuse me. There were also two elderly men who were burned. That's Idriz Xhemajli and Shaban Rexhepi, and they were burned on a tractor in the yard of Muharrem Osmani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now please tell us how long the Serb forces stayed in Izbica.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 28th and until 9.00 a.m. on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you present in the woods overlooking the village until their departure?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. The first two days I was towards the west, and on the last day I was in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then, following the withdrawal of the forces, go and inspect the victims? And I don't want detailed accounts because we're going to see this in the video which will be produced through a witness coming later this week, Dr. Loshi.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in summary, the injuries you found were consistent with being killed how?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were all killed by heavy weapons, by semi-automatic rifles. And because of the close range, the bodies were very badly damaged. I found people alive three days later, and one of these is Sedik Hoti, and Haxhi Krasniqi. And in the first group I met him. Sadik Hoti died, whereas Haxhi Krasniqi is still alive. And among the pile of -- the first pile of corpses -- I came from the east and this was the first group that I came across. I was with two other friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. It shows no disrespect by either you, by the Prosecution, or by the Court, that we cannot deal with every individual victim. It is enough, for our purposes, that we deal with the generality of what you are describing. But as a matter of appropriate respect, I think one of the victims was your Uncle Tahir's son, Xhemajli Idriz; is that correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. Idriz Xhemajli. Yes. He's my first cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you organised a commission for the burial of the victims, and you tried to keep the work within a comparatively limited number of people.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were some 85 individuals who were involved in digging the graves by hand and burying the dead; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many -- how many bodies were buried in the field that was chosen for the burial site?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There on the west, where the majority were killed, a fellow villager had an acre of land and said that he would -- he would give this land as a gift to the martyrs, and he told us to bury these people as soon as possible, and they were very nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many were buried?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: His name was Hamdi Bajrami.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many were buried?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, 118 were buried, and on the 1st of April, nine more were buried. So in all, there were 127 people buried. And there were 32 people from Izbica alone who were killed, and the others were from other villages up to 80 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- there were three individuals buried in Kladernica, I think Kladernica, I think, and they having been killed by a hand grenade thrown into a house where they were staying in Izbica and their surname being Beka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Haxhi Beka, Sale Beka and Shpresa Beka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If what I've said is correct just say and we can move on?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included and of significance, obviously in your view, and it may be of significance, including amongst those killed was somebody called Rrahim Tahiri along with his brother Brahim Tahiri, but tell us about Rrahim Tahiri's mobility and state of health.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And age.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Rrahim Tahiri was in a wheelchair, and his brother Brahim was pushing it. And during the journey with the column of women at one edge of Izbica they came across Serbian forces, and they were executed. He was educated -- he was executed in a wheelchair. They were over 70 years old. I buried these two with my own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us already and I'm now on page 7 of the statement, any who are following it, you told us also of the woman who was burnt to death, burnt on the back of the tractor, and I think she had had limited mobility, is that correct, and was partially paralysed?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That's right. I said before she was with Qerime Hajra.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, when burying these bodies, did you check their identities?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. All of those whom the other citizens didn't know, I had to identify them. And I checked their pocket, their bodies to see if they had any documents. And those who didn't have any documents, I described their clothes or the things they had in their pockets. And sometimes somebody would come out and identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able by those methods to identify all or nearly all of the people you buried?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were all identified in time, but there was only one who was not identified by the time came to bury them on 1st of April. He has been identified since. This was Shyqem Dobra from Krusheve. In his pocket --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause please, Mr. Xhemajli. Pause please. Did you make notes in your own pocketbook of the names of the people you were burying as you came to identify them?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you had your notes reflected in a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not completely translated yet, indeed at all, I think, but it is largely a list of names. And although we have a list of names on pages 7 and 8 of the statement, it's probably easier, quicker and more appropriate to produce the list as an exhibit rather than rely on production of the statement. I'm content to do it either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Produce the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can produce this document, please, and of course we will -- the parts that are not translated will be translated. And this list is differently ordered from the list in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to explain something. May I explain this, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's to do with the list, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't -- I'm not receiving an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want to explain something. If you would briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just three words. The -- in the -- in the committee for the burial, there were three of us, and it was Afrim Xhemajli who prepared the list, and there were other two who kept order during the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you look, please, at this document which is before you on the desk?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- can another version be laid on the overhead projector for those viewing. Can we, in due course, have a number for it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can have a number temporarily, but it must be translated before it is formally exhibited. Let's have a number now then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Temporary number will be Prosecutors Exhibit 286.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much and I will arrange for its translation to be speeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a document prepared by you or in any event under your organisation? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: This document was prepared from notes in my notebook and tidied up to present to you. If you need a photocopy, I can provide you one, but I can't give you my original notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your notebook is available for inspection today, but you wish to retain it. This document lists those who died in the massacre at Izbica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while we are looking at the document. Mr. Xhemajli, you said that Idriz Xhemajli was your first cousin, son of your uncle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His age was 90 -- 76 at the time? He was born in 1926?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've made some reference to this already, but can you please help us a little further? Included in these people who died were there men who you understood to have been mentally handicapped? If so, how many of them?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were eight in all. I could give you their names. Becir Llausha.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's enough that you give the number. Thank you. The woods in which you had been staying, were they also home to many villagers from the surrounding area at this time, the end of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were other forces but they were in the woods, whereas looking directly at the massacre, I was by myself, although I did have some friends at a greater distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. My mistake. I'll go back and ask the question again. You were in some woods. You've told us about them, woods surrounding these villages. Did those woods provide home and shelter to civilians, to villagers, at the end of March of 1999? And did you help them try and get some food?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I helped them all, both the military and the population. And I've got lists of people to whom I gave food, flour, oil, and also medicines. And I took people to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Regardless of whether they were civilians or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. How many civilians, in your estimation, were using the surrounding woods for refuge?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said before that there were about 4.500 to 5.000 in the meadows. No doubt there were about 2.000 in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to pass over events where members of the KLA as fighting forces were killed, but tell us this: Did there come a time when a large number of people left the woods for Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of them. Eighty per cent of those who were civilians in the woods, they fled to Montenegro, to Rozaje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was there any particular incident that led them to do that or was it just a collective decision that the time had come to go?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: This case on the 28th of March there were Serb forces, and on the 13th of May near Izbica at 5.00 in the morning and then at 2.00 there were infantry forces. So according to the witnesses there, there were a lot -- there was a lot of shelling all day. Everyone was up in the hills. And in the Alia neighbourhood there were two civilians. They were both taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are going into more detail than we need or that we can probably understand at this speed. It's not necessary for the detail.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A large number of people left for Montenegro. Did then just go of their own decision-making or was there something that caused them to go? Did something happen in general terms that caused them to go to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were forced to go by Serb forces. They were being beaten every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is this in the woods or is this in the towns -- not the towns, in the villages that people were being beaten by the Serb forces and thus forced to make their way to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Even women were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is: Was this happening in the woods or was this happening in the villages?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, no. It was -- people were taken from the Alia neighbourhood, and then they were forced to line up against a wall. And they were robbed. Things were taken out of their pockets. And in the Xhemala [phoen] neighbourhood 12 people were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So these events were happening in the villages. Now tell us what happened in the woods. Did they also leave and make their way to Montenegro? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. They all went after the killings. Everyone left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was the killings that were happening else where that led to these people leaving the woods and going to Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Izbica itself which had been left by the Serb forces and in which you'd been able to bury this large number of people, was it subject to a renewed attack in the form of shelling?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No. There was no more shelling, no more bombing. There was shelling, though, from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when did that happen, what day or date, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That was on the 11th of May there were over 200 shells which were fired at the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the village inhabited at this stage by any or many people?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were still some of the people. But by the 11th of May, most of the people left and went to Montenegro and to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following the -- this shelling on the 11th of May of Izbica with over 200 shells, did Serb forces arrive on foot?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, at 2.00 Serb infantry arrived, and they took 12 civilians from the Alia neighbourhood and executed them. At 3.15 in the afternoon I entered the village with three friends, and we found the bodies of those executed. Ismet Arif Mermullaku and Milazim Shala, who -- one of them died almost -- right after that, after being given first aid, whereas Milazim died the next day in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have listed in your statement at page 9 the 12 people concerned who died who were buried in the Izbica graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would rely on that list to provide the names, if it's necessary, for them to be identified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The next day on the 12th, we buried them all. We didn't have instruments. We didn't have tools to carry them or -- it was night. So we just put them on a wagon and -- on a wagon and carried them away and buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later, a couple of weeks later, on the 29th of May did the Serbs return to Izbica, now a deserted village?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did they do on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: On the 28th and the 29th and the 30th, they set up bases on the hills and surrounded the whole village of Izbica. And on the 31st of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to the 31st of May, in order to deal with things chronologically, although there were no people in the village, were there livestock, animals, horses, and one thing or another there?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The animals were all alone, had been abandoned, and at 12.15 that day, they killed all the animals in the village. One hundred and fifty animals were killed. And on the 31st of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: -- after they took up positions on the hills, around the hills, on the hills, they began to bury the bodies from -- they began to dig up the bodies and then they stopped. They started to exhume them, but they didn't exhume them all, whereas on the 1st of June, the forces didn't move from their positions. And on the 2nd of June, an excavator arrived and exhumed all the bodies. The exhumation lasted two days, until 1400 hours on the 3rd. They took all the bodies in a truck and took them away towards the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to the site where the bodies had been buried?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were all taken away, and they tried to hide the site a bit, but they weren't able to because we had recordings. We had evidence. So after one crime, they committed another one. And these --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, I understand the temptation, but all we need is the straightforward facts. They tried to cover the site by what, using a bulldozer or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. They covered it up with a -- with a bulldozer, with an excavator. And to eradicate all the traces, they took away all the blankets and the planks and also the wooden stakes with the names on, and they put them on a trailer and set them on fire. But fortunately, a third party arrived and extinguished the fire and preserved this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you didn't know at the time where the bodies were taken. But later, between December 1999 or during December 1999, were bodies found in and around the area at Mitrovica? And of those, 200 bodies in all, had some, 42, been positively identified by relations as having come from the Izbica graveyard?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your witness statement, you were able to name 20 of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I have 38 names now, original names, which coincide -- there was a coincidence between the names of the massacres and the names of the recovered bodies. And some of -- some witnesses have stated that the blanket of one was found in Belgrade. He was one of the people who was buried in Izbica, and you can find his name on the list here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would propose, in order that there should be no problem -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Musliu his name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would propose, in order there be no problem later, is that if in due course the totality of the witness statement is not produced as an exhibit, that pages 9 and 10 may be produced as a separate exhibit at the end of re-examination simply for the purposes of the lists that they contain. Otherwise, we've got to go through lots of names in a way that will take time and be duplicative of work already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, there's one other topic I want you to help us with, please, Mr. Xhemajli.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not covered in the statement or the summary, Your Honour. It only came to notice to me yesterday. And I'll get the witness to explain it and to deal, insofar as we can, with the video that I'm in a position to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, did you watch the television in the days and months after these events and see various broadcasts that concerned Izbica? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there one broadcast involving a government official of some kind where the very existence of Izbica as a village was denied? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this on Serbian television, Belgrade television, on the 18th of April, 1999. They denied the massacre and said there was supposedly no village called Izbica and only 12 houses with 70 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: And in that recording, they produced two Serbian witnesses from the village of Bjelica who introduced themselves -- the first supposedly as Bajram Shala, and the second supposedly as Nesir Shala. And these Serbs who introduced themselves with Albanian names are Miroslav Sabic, and Dusan Sabic. These two on this videocassette say that there were no graves, nobody was killed, and that we are plowing the fields and all these are lies. This was cooked up in the kitchen of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No comments, thank you. Now, not too fast because this is coming new to the learned Judges. So there's a denial that Izbica existed, and then there's a broadcast involving two men purporting to be Albanians who deny that the massacre ever happened. Is that correct, to begin with?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the video that you've provided and that's been extracted for the purposes of this hearing this very morning, does the video contain interviews between yourself and the real Albanians whose names had been given by these two men you say were Serbs, the real Albanians denying that what was accredited to them was accurate?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, does the video that you've produced contain footage of one of the men purporting to be an Albanian but actually seen to be carrying arms and operating as a Serb soldier or policeman or something of that kind?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, the video exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's happened is the video has been worked on this morning. The total video, which I can produce, would take 30 minutes and 18 seconds, and I don't intend to use that amount of time or seek to do so. It has yet to be translated, so it doesn't have a transcript with it. But the segments of it, I have now identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, nobody has put this in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This goes to another issue. This is, of course, material that may prove of significance in the evidence about propaganda generally when that comes for consideration in the case as a whole. But if Your Honour means it hasn't been put in issue in that it hasn't been challenged, quite right. We could simply postpone using the actual video until after cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That would seem sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will certainly have it served on the accused and the amici in any event today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We don't want to waste too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in which case, I think that concludes all I need to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Mr. Xhemajli, we are going to adjourn for 20 minutes. During the adjournment, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. If you could be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the examination-in-chief, Mr. Nice quite pompously announced some tapes in which, according to what he stated, it can be seen that this is some kind of propaganda or so. I don't know how it is possible for me to start the cross-examination at all until we see those tapes. I don't see any reason why these tapes shouldn't be shown so that we can see what this is all about. There are interpreters here. If there is no translation, we will hear the translation in the same way that everything that goes on in this room is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can go on with your cross-examination. If there comes a time when you put things in issue, that is you challenge that this incident occurred, then the tapes, in due course, can be played. Now, you're to have an hour and a quarter to cross-examine this witness. You should begin now. You can have a few minutes in the morning. If the Prosecution are going to rely on the tape, we will have it with a proper translation, and we will -- you can ask some questions about it tomorrow. It's a side issue, Mr. Milosevic. It's a totally side issue to this witness's evidence. It's not central to it at all, so there's no reason why you can't begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this testimony is a farce just like this whole operation that you call a trial, because there was no execution in Izbica. This is a pure fabrication, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Get on with your cross-examination. Put it to the witness if that's what you say. Let him answer it. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is so obvious. There isn't a single officer of the Yugoslav army or police who could order the execution of civilians nor soldiers or police officers who would carry out such an order even if it existed. It's pure nonsense. But since you insist that I start the cross-examination, I will start it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And don't waste time by making comments. It will all be deducted from your time in cross-examination. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please explain to me, Mr. Xhemajli, why you are masked with a beard and dark glasses?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I have -- I wear a beard as a symbol of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about the dark glasses. Why are you wearing them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My eyesight is not very good. I need the glasses to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since when has your eyesight not been very good?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Since after the war. It started during the war, but mostly after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how is it that your sight is helped by dark glasses? I understand that magnifying lenses help, but how do dark lenses help?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are they medically prescribed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which doctor prescribed those glasses for you?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: What is that -- what business is that of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, because you are wearing dark glasses. It is not normal for a witness in a court to wear dark glasses. It is only because Mr. Nice explained that you had some medical condition that we allowed it. Now, if you don't want to give the doctor's name, you can tell us where he comes from, who he is, something about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the medical centre in Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the findings from this doctor, the diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Here you mean? What would you need that for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, I don't have them here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, please. I demand that this witness be subject to an ophthalmological examination so that we can determine what is correct and what is not, because I am voicing doubts over the reasons that were stated for which he is wearing dark glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't have such an examination now. We hear what you say. We hear the Prosecution do. No doubt if they want to support the witnesses evidence, they will go about doing so, but at the moment we've heard what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that there were 5.000 people on this meadow and that there were another 2.000 in the woods. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were up to 5.000 in the meadows. That's the number. Men mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And about 2.000 in the woods, is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, then, how is it possible that out of these 5.000 on the meadow and out of those 2.000 in the woods only you alone saw some kind of alleged execution, and those other 4.999 in the meadow and 1.999 in the woods, nobody else saw anything? And you also happened to be the commander of a pretty large unit. How is this possible?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It is possible. They all saw the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the only witness of that alleged execution here was Milazim Thaci, who according to what he said was shot by a heavy machine-gun from a distance of seven metres and that he wasn't even touched?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. The witness can't comment on what some other witness said. You know quite well that that is a matter for argument which you can put to us. What you can ask this witness about is what he saw himself or what he heard himself, but he can't comment on what somebody else said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you accepted as an exhibit here the photograph of the shirt of this Milazim Thaci which has three holes. So the photograph of his alleged shirt with three bullet holes, while he wasn't even grazed by a single bullet with the explanation that he was saved by God. Only God didn't save his shirt. And you are asking for someone to believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's nothing to do with this witness. Now, ask this witness some relevant questions if you've got any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will go in order. I have plenty of relevant questions, and I think that I was given less time than Nice was given, but this is your decision. We will start from the beginning of his statement. In view of the fact that I received the statement only in English and I don't have it in B/C/S, I will quote from the English text that you provided to me. You claim, Mr. Xhemajli, that Serbs --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't want you to call me mister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look, Mr. Xhemajli. What is normal in this court is that people are called mister. It's a matter of politeness. Now, let us get on with it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You were going to read something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that Serbs did not want to register newborn Albanian children by their names but that they gave them Serb names by adding "vic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It is correct. My son was born in 1992. I wanted to call him Alban, but they wouldn't allow me. And his birth has not been registered even to this day. I didn't want to register him in Cyrillic because I gave him his name myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assert that the documents received by citizens in Kosovo and Metohija were not both in the Serb and Albanian languages? Are you claiming that they were only in the Serb language?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I'm talking about after 1989. After -- after the overthrow of the autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm also talking about after 1989, and I claim that the documents that Albanians got in Kosovo were in the Albanian language as well, not only in the Serb language. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I never had anything to do with them. I never saw a single document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If never saw a single document, how can you claim that they were only in the Serb language and not in Albanian as well?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I know very well what they were like. So do you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I know. I know that they are in Serbian and Albanian. And where Turks live they're also in the Turkish language. Where Bulgarians live also in the Bulgarian language. Where Hungarians lived also in the Hungarian language. That is the way it is all over Serbia; is that right or is that not right, Mr. Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: During that period everything was Serbian. There was nothing Albanian at all. Kosova at that time was reduced to level of a little local municipality. They took away the government, the Executive Council. All the schools were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, never mind the government and the Executive Council now. I'm talking to you about documents because you spoke about documents and said that the documents were not in both languages. You say that they were only in the Serb language. Is that your assertion? And then let us go on.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: After 1990 they were only in the Serbian language. I'm talking about the municipality of Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's easy to prove. So we're not going to dwell on that any longer. Tell us, please, who is this that Serbs added "vic" to their names to in order to make them Serbian? Can you mention the name of at least one Albanian child whose name was changed by the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were many cases of this kind. There were even cases before 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you say that there are many such cases, give me one example of a person, of an Albanian person whose name the Serb authorities did not want to register as it is but they registered it in the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: For instance, instead of calling me by my name Xhemajli, they called me Xhemaliaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Xhemaliaj, that's also Albanian to the best of my knowledge. It's not Serbian in any case?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, there's no "a-j" in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does is say Xhemaliaj in your documents?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, Albanian is Xhemajli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How come you told that story in your statement that they added "vic" because you said that they added "vic." What would your last name look like if "vic" were added to it Xhemajlivic? Is that what it says in any one of your IDs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what have I come to be asked about? I have come to be asked about the massacre and what is in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is relevant. It goes to your credibility. You have said there was a practice of adding v-i-c at the end of Albanian names to make them Serb. And what you're being asked is to give some examples and if you can, you should. If you're not able to, then I think it does cast some doubt on your credibility. Give an actual example. Do you know of any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He himself said it. He said Xhemajlivic. He said it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Can you give an actual example of a person that you know, an Albanian whose name was changed to the Serb version by adding v-i-c? Somebody that you knew, not speaking generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Xhemajlivic. You had it in every document. But they burnt them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that was in your documents and then these documents were burned.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They were left with nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you didn't mention that in your statement, that they burned your documents?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No doubt I should have mentioned it, but how I overlooked it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. This is quite clear. You claim in paragraph 8, page 2, and on page 3 in the first paragraph of this English version of your statement that on the 28th of February 1998 in Likoshane and Cirez the Serb forces massacred 24 villagers, mainly members of the Ahmetaj and Sejdiu families. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the villagers of Likoshane and Cirez were the greatest strongholds of the KLA at the time?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That is not true. At that time, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when were they? At what time?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Later. It was a small group at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, later. Only a small group at that time. And do you know that at that time very fierce fighting was taking place between the members of the KLA and the police?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: In which place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely in Likoshane and Cirez.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: What were Serbian forces looking for there? It's an Albanian village there, and they had no business there. They had done nothing to anybody. They were working their own land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that's a different matter. That is a different matter, Mr. Xhemajli. And do you know that all the persons who were killed were armed members of the KLA, precisely in Likoshan and Cirez, that you have referred to, saying that civilians were massacred there? All the persons killed were armed members of the KLA. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's not true. And anybody can testify to that in front of the Tribunal. There was not a single KLA soldier who was killed. There were women, children, pregnant women. Anybody can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for witnesses, you are famous for that, but you say that after the funerals of the members of the Ahmetaj and Sejdiu families, you became an active member and a commander in the village of Kastriot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, I was an ordinary soldier. I wasn't a commander. Nobody had the right to call me a commander. I became a member of the KLA, of the liberation army. And if -- if it hadn't been for the other side, the KLA would never have been founded because it's the acts of crimes and maltreatment that you carried out and all the crimes you carried out and denying us all our rights. That's why the KLA came to be born.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, do try to answer only my questions. Please, don't make speeches. On page 3 of your statement, you say: "[In Enlish] I volunteered and joined the KLA on 13th of March, 1998. I became a member of Kastriot village KLA. Even though I had no prior military experience, I was made commander of my unit." [Interpretation] Therefore, what is correct, what you are claiming right now, or what you wrote down here that I asked you about, that you became a commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said before I was an ordinary soldier; and in time, I became an officer in charge of a squad, and later, an officer in the brigade. But in stages, not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That cannot be seen from your statement. I've read the entire sentence to you. And in the same sentence you say that you became a commander of the KLA, in the same sentence where you refer to joining the KLA and generally speaking. Now, let's move on from there. You say yourself that your activities at that time meant taking action against members of the police in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Of course, when Serbian forces came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how many such actions were undertaken by your unit in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There was a need to take action, but for defensive purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you how many such actions were taken by your unit in 1998.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I gave a very exact reply. We didn't -- we didn't undertake actions. We defended our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who is this that you were defending your homes from in 1998 when it is well known that you were killing soldiers, policemen, mailmen, civilians, Serbs, Albanians, everybody, from ambushes?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Anybody who looted and attacked were killed, but we didn't go and attack you. You attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So when you shoot at a police vehicle that is moving down a road, in your opinion, that is defence from some kind of violence. Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, because it's defence. It depends who's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many Serb policemen did you kill or wound in these actions? Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I -- no, I'm not competent to answer that question. I don't know any numbers. I'm not competent to answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in these actions, did you manage to take prisoner, any prisoners from among the policemen?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: We didn't. Others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was their fate then when they were taken prisoner by the others?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The fate of the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What happened to these policemen that you had kidnapped? What did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It was other superior organs which dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So it was your superior organs that ordered the torture and killing of policemen. You personally did not take part in any such thing?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, I didn't. They were sent on to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, page 3, you complain for the most part that at first, your men were not trained enough to handle the weapons that you had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them had done military service; but most of them, they hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Xhemajli, that you acquired experience precisely in these terrorist actions that you took against the police, against the legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That is not terrorism. Your side was the terrorism. They killed old men and women, children; destroyed houses, yards, chickens, livestock, everything that was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about experience, and you yourself know that what you've been saying about children and old people are not true. We've heard these stories already. You say that towards the end of 1998, you received large amounts of smuggled weapons. Tell me, what kind of weapons are these?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: First of all, what you're saying, these are not fairy tales. These are documents. They exist recorded on video. It's well known who did these things. It's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about smuggled weapons, Mr. Xhemajli.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The weapons were brought in many ways, which any -- any way we could. We weren't able to select our weapons. We were confronting tanks and aeroplanes. We weren't able to match automatic rifles with automatic rifles. We were defending ourselves. We didn't choose war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons did your unit have at the end of 1998 and beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Machine-guns, semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that already towards the end of the summer of 1998 you had heavy machine-guns, recoilless guns, sniper guns, et cetera; is that correct? Mortars?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: 12.5 machine-guns; but others, no. No mortars. Here and there, there were some semi-automatics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that the KLA had cooperation, constant contacts with the members of the OSCE. What was this cooperation reflected in?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said cooperation. I said -- didn't say "cooperation." I said good relations. Cooperation is one thing; good relations are another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What were these good relations reflected in?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They helped the people. We used to talk together. We organised things for victims, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me lead -- let me read a sentence of your own here. "[In English] The KLA cooperated with them, and they were constantly in contact with the OSCE." [Interpretation] And the sentence before that: "[In English] In October 1998, the OSCE came into Kosovo to monitor the situation." [Interpretation] And then you said: "[In English] The KLA cooperated with them ..." [Interpretation] So what did this cooperation consist of?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said during that pause when the agreement was in force, there were people who were killed. And we had a good form of understanding with these people. We didn't have cooperation. Some people were unable to return to their own homes, so we used them as intermediaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about cooperation between the KLA and the OSCE mission. That's what it says in your own sentence: "The KLA cooperated with them." You are not talking about civilian cooperation; you're talking about the cooperation between the KLA and the OSCE. So I'm asking you about that cooperation specifically. I'm not making a general point here.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The KLA talked to the OSCE and told them of certain cases in which the people were worried, and they were unable to return their own homes. And they would tell OSCE -- they would say that so-and-so is unable to return to his home and can something be done about it. This wasn't actual cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If it is so, if it is the way you're putting it now, then explain the following to me: As a member of the KLA and as one of the commanders, as we have ascertained, you say, in paragraph 6 on page 3, that NATO aggression against the FRY took place at the right time because the KLA needed assistance. Is that right, or is that not right? Is that what you've stated or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's not true that -- NATO helped us. I didn't talk about NATO aggression. NATO helped us. They were supporting the people directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "[In English] On 24th of March, 1999, NATO commenced its offensive against Serbia. It was very welcome at this time. The KLA wasn't so strong then and needed help." [Interpretation] Does that mean that NATO precisely helped you -- does that mean that NATO precisely helped you?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: They helped the people of Kosova. They rescued them from a catastrophe. I am a member of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that NATO helped you, as you put it, in carrying out your separatist objectives by way of terrorism against the legal authorities? Is that right, or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's not true that the -- that NATO helped the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the KLA have coordinated activities with NATO, and did the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia strengthen the position of the KLA and your terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: You must ask somebody else because I was a very small character. I was a very minor player in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about any cooperation with the representatives of the OSCE after they withdrew from Kosovo? And if so, what did these contacts consist of and in which way were these contacts materialised?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Are you talking about the OSCE or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about side that conducted war against us, including certain members of the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Once again, please. Mixed it up completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether after the withdrawal of the OSCE mission from Kosovo, you had cooperation and contacts with their representatives; and if so, in what way were these contacts carried out? How did they happen?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I -- how could I have contact with them when we know that on 19th of March, you were -- you threw them out? You threw them out of Kosova, threw them out of Yugoslavia, and there was no more contact with them. The last one went out on the 19th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are claiming that we threw them out.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Of course. You threw them out because you blamed them for the report on Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have to explain that further. That is quite all right for you to have such an explanation. Could you please tell me, you're claiming on page 3, in paragraph 2, that only a small number of KLA members had uniforms, and you say even at the end of the war many were not wearing uniforms, did not have uniforms. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: It's true that a majority did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the majority did not have uniforms. Before that, we noted that you received large quantities. Previously we noted that you received large quantities of weapons. So your comrades in arms who were not wearing uniforms but all of you had weapons, large quantities of weapons. Do you consider them civilians or fighters? Or I would call them terrorists, of course. Do you consider them to be civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: We know very well who the terrorists were, they were the other side. First of all, I didn't say that the majority were in civilian clothes but a large part didn't have uniforms. They had guns, but they didn't have uniforms, but it wasn't the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said a majority a little while ago, but even a large part is sufficient for us to be able to note that a large part fought in civilian clothes and killed in civilian clothes. Could you please tell me if it's true that in the period from the 24th of March to the 29th of March in the area of Srbica, Izbica, Drenice, Leqina and so on very intensive fighting was conducted between the numerous forces of the KLA and our forces? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I can't answer if your questions are so long. You never stop. I can give you a clear and short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you were looking at the map with Mr. Nice, you described a series of villages. You mentioned Turiceve, Izbica, Srbica, Leqina, and so on. Is it true that at that time from the 24th of March to the 29th of March very intense fighting was conducted between the numerous KLA forces and our forces? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I didn't mention Turiceve, Leqina, Kastriot, Izbica, Qitak, but not -- I did mention but not Turiceve. There were -- there was fighting. Yes, of course. If people come and attack you, you have to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is your explanation, that somebody came to attack you. Is it true that at that time in that region the 111th, 112th, 113th, 114th, 140th and 145th Brigade of the KLA were present in that territory and were active? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The last two were not in Drenice at all, the last two you mentioned. The first three do exist. They did exist. But if we're talking about all of Drenica or are we talking about just my little area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Drenica. This is where the fighting was conducted. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: But Drenica is a big region. There are 52 different villages. It's a big area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The size can be seen, but is it true that there were these six KLA brigades there in that territory and they were fighting against the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Eleven, 12, 13 that's three, just three. Where do you get the six from? The last two said don't exist, did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 114th, the 140th and the 145th and another three. Were they there?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said it already. 11, 12, and 13 did exist in Drenica. The others, no, they weren't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were three brigades there. So does that mean that there were about 2.500 armed KLA members there at that time? Is that a correct figure?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: If we're talking about all of Drenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to this alleged event of yours. You claim on page 5, in paragraph 2 that from a distance of about 700 metres -- now you stated 600, but it doesn't change very much -- heard how our soldiers were practically setting the tariff for a life, a house, or a vehicle. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know that money was demanded, extorted. I know that they talked about different sums. And the survivors of the massacre did explain that to me, that there were different tariffs about the money, for a car, for a house, it was different. But there was a lot of looting. But other people have said this before me. There are a lot of people who have declared that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There should be no doubt about that. Everybody could see that. There is a large number of false witnesses here, KLA members. But you said this. My question is different, though. You heard that they were demanding 1.000 German marks for their lives to be spared, 1.000 for their family, 1.000 for a house, 50 to 100 for their tractors and vehicles, and you heard all of that from a distance of 600 metres. You heard them setting these prices. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No. No. They told me -- the survivors told me, the people who survived, said that on the 28th of March, a lot of people could not get to Albania. They were returned, the women and children. They were returned a week later. And on the 11th of May, they took them again, all the women, all the females and the children, as a second group in to houses. The latter was called -- of Avdija's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you clarify this for me? You didn't hear this but you were told this later, the next day or on subsequent days; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There was no need. My family was involved in this. It wasn't hearsay at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm just asking you. Could you please respond precisely yes or no. Did you hear this or not? Our police officers and soldiers demanding money, did you hear that or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I heard them saying something, but I don't know exactly what they said. Later it was explained to me what they'd said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you didn't hear it but you were told about it. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you state here that you heard this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with this issue. He's given his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that you, from a distance far away, that you were able to hear. How were you, with your poor eyesight, able to see what happened at such a distance?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: From the noise. There was shouting, crying and screaming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked how could you see with your poor eyesight. How were you able to see at such a distance what was happening? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My eyesight was better at that time. It got worse after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And since you described that out of those 5.000 people who were present plus the 2.000 who were in the woods, you were the only one who saw that. Could you please tell me where the other members of your KLA unit were at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: That's not -- it's not true that I was the only one who saw it. These terrible events were witnessed by many people. But I was the person chosen to come here to give a statement. But there are others. There are a lot of other people who saw it, but they couldn't all come here. Two thousand people couldn't come here to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have no doubt that you are able to send several thousand people to testify even that I myself was present there. I wrote down when Mr. Nice asked you, and you responded that this massacre, you saw this massacre by yourself, alone, the commander of the unit, the villagers. There is no unit, there are no villagers. You were watching this by yourself?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: From the position I was at in the west, I was alone at that moment for a short while. But afterwards, a lot of people were there. They returned, and they told me about it too. I was on the western side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have it noted here that you say that according to the testimony of witnesses Serbian forces surrounded Izbica. Two civilians were killed. You stated this spontaneously now even though this wasn't written down. But please, could you respond? Why did those 5.000 civilians walk out into the meadow? You said that they walked out there by themselves, that nobody forced them to do that. So why did they come out to that meadow?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: The men went out, and then the women -- there were a lot of people who were disabled. There were old people. There were children. They couldn't go up into the mountains, so they thought that they would gather together because they would be safer with all the old people. But you didn't care about them. If they had known, they would have left for the mountains too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you respond to my question, please, Mr. Xhemajli. Why did you take refuge in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that. He's explained why he says they went there. Now, move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, in order to be quite precise, did you take refuge in the meadow so that you would be in a large visible group because you were fleeing from the bombing? Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He wasn't in the meadow himself. The others were in the meadow. He was on a hill in the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Why did -- I won't say why did you, but why did they go to the meadow? Did they go to that meadow in such a large group in order to protect themselves from the bombing, in order to be visible as a large group, to be visible as civilians? Because previously quite heavy bombing had taken place. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I wasn't there. It was the population which gathered together. There was shelling and bombing in the houses, so they had to leave. And they hoped that Serb forces, seeing them, would not kill them. The people surrendered. They went out in the meadows, the women and the children. But the UCK, the KLA, was up in the mountains. They were not with them. They withdrew because of Serb forces, not because of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's understand one another properly, Mr. Xhemajli. Awhile ago, in response to a request by Mr. Nice to describe something, you stated, and I wrote it down -- it's in the transcript, line 615809. You said there was no more bombing, and then you continued to explain about the shelling. When you say there was no more bombing, does that mean that there was bombing before? So can I conclude that the people fled to the meadow because NATO was bombing the village? Is this true, Mr. Xhemajli, or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must divide that up. He said earlier that it wasn't because of the NATO bombing. But the first question is this: Was there NATO bombing in the area before this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO started bombing on the 24th of March. This was on the 28th of March. It's not true that we fled from NATO bombing. NATO didn't bomb. It was the shelling by Serb forces we fled from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said spontaneously that there was no more bombing. So this means there was some bombing before that, otherwise you wouldn't have put it like that.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I think I made myself clear. In Izbica there was no NATO bombing at all. There was shelling from your forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't it perhaps happen like this: People had fled the bombing, they went to the meadow in order to be visible from the air, a large group of civilians, and that the consequence of that bombing are these burnt bodies in tractors and you are attributing these NATO crimes to the Serbian forces? Didn't that event happen like that, Mr. Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that at all. You can change things around the way you want, but that's not what it was. That's what you did. It was your action. Your hands were behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. You stated today that out of those 5.000 people in the meadow, they separated out all the men, and you said they did this one by one. One by one. That is exactly what you had said, and I wrote that down.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, one by one. They took them out one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One by one. Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Couldn't -- they couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that out of 5.000 citizens there were only 150 men?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Because the young men didn't want to go out into the meadow. They headed for the -- for the hills. It was only the women and the children and the handicapped and the old, the invalids, the mentally ill who were out in the meadow there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that group of 5.000 people comprised only 2.5 per cent of men and 97.5 were women and children. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes. Of all the men who were in that group, only 16 survived. Only 16 survived. Yes, I've heard that -- now I've just heard that a seventeenth did survive. Others were wounded. Fourteen were wounded. And they had wounds on their clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not talking about that right now. I'm asking you, does it seem logical to you your claim that out of 5.000 people there are only 150 men, only 2 per cent men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not a proper question as to whether it's logical or not. That's his evidence. It doesn't matter whether it's logical or not. He's given it. He says that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But his claim is illogical to such an extent that it's obviously a falsehood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point arguing like that. You've heard his evidence. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you please explain to me how you, from the distance that you were at, it says here 700 and you've stated that it was 600 metres, how did you manage to count the exact number of men that you claim were divided into two groups? And why did you count them at all?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Mr. May, firstly, he's lying. And I'm being offended here. I feel offended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Xhemajli, don't be offended. You're just giving evidence. You're telling us what happened. The accused is entitled to ask questions however offensive you might find them or irritating. If you just answer them, we'll get on more quickly. What he's asking is: How were you able to count them? Perhaps you can just explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean, the dead bodies or the people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people, because you say that you saw from a distance of 700 metres, you saw them being separated and that you counted how many of them there were. Please read your statement so that you can see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly how many were divided up, but I know how many survived. There were 16 who survived of all the men who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I understood during the examination-in-chief, you explained that you only saw them being separated and that you did not see them being shot. And later, you said that you saw a group of 30 being shot. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was no distinction. He said in his evidence that he saw the group of, I think, 39 being shot. That was his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the 39 dead, but I didn't know exactly how many there were from the whole -- how many there were in the whole group, but I saw there were 39 who were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw these 39 people. You saw them personally being shot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many members of our forces were there that you claimed carried this out? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: There were four who drove the whole group out into the meadow, and there were others around in the surrounding area. Mr. May, they could have -- the group, the whole group, could have stopped the execution of the 39 people, but they were with their families there and they didn't dare to intervene because they would -- their families would have been executed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You didn't answer my question. So there were four police officers and how many others were there also?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: Twenty. There were 20, not four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, 20. So can you please explain to me how is it that you, with your unit, did not rush to help your fellow citizens out when there were only 20 police officers there who allegedly organised and carried out the execution of some 150 people according to you? How can this be? One person would help when there were only 20 people in question. How is it that you did not intervene, you and your unit?

utterances.speaker: SADIK XHEMAJLI
utterances.text: I said that 20 people committed the execution, but there were a lot of other forces. But it was only 20 who did the execution. There were hundreds of other troops. The KLA couldn't intervene because it -- had it shot, it would have shot into the crowd. We had to be very careful. We didn't want to shoot because we would have shot into the people and wounded people. There was KLA there, but because of the family members there, we couldn't intervene. There is a clean -- clean fighting and dirty fighting. The Serb police were always fighting with the population, with the civilian population, dirty war, but we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We know that story. It is quite untrue. My question was different, however. How is it that you see that they are about to shoot your fellow citizens and you don't rush to help them, and your entire KLA unit is close at hand and you do not wish to help them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness has answered that. He's given his answer. Just look at the last one he gave. We're going to adjourn now. The time has come. Mr. Xhemajli, would you be back, please, tomorrow to conclude your examination. Mr. Milosevic, we will give you ten minutes more tomorrow morning, ten minutes more, in which case you will have had longer than the Prosecution. We will allow the Prosecution to produce the video since this whole incident has now been put into issue and it's suggested it's a fabrication. We will allow the video to be produced, and we will allow you, Mr. Milosevic, to ask some more questions related purely to that video and nothing else. Very well. All that 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. Are you giving me ten minutes more or are you giving me only ten minutes tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to give you ten minutes more to conclude your examination. We will then see the video. We will allow you to ask some questions about that but purely limited to the video in addition to the other questions you may ask. Yes. Of course we will allow the amicus to ask some questions if there are any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'll try and take the video in a summary form. Maybe, therefore, it would be helpful for the accused if he has the time and opportunity to see -- to view the video this afternoon. I'll make sure we get it to him. I will do my best to make sure that there is a transcript available to allow things to be taken swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of August, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
